1 Introduction

Most multimodal models acquire visual understanding from a vision encoder pretrained for a separate objective, such as image recognition or image–text alignment, rather than from being trained directly with the multimodal backbone that uses its features (He et al., 2016; Radford et al., 2021; Tschannen et al., 2025; Siméoni et al., 2026; Tschannen et al., 2023). Multimodal training has progressed from freezing this encoder (Alayrac et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2023; Muse Glimmer Team, 2026) to updating it (Beyer et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025a), but encoder pretraining has remained a separate stage. Recent recipes bring vision and language closer by discarding parts of the pretrained encoder setup: Kimi K3 trains a vision encoder from scratch jointly with the multimodal backbone (Kimi Team, 2026b), and encoder-free models directly process pixel patches, forcing visual encoding to be learned entirely within the backbone (Adept AI, 2023; Diao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026; Gemma Team, 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a). Each recipe implies a different answer to what the vision encoder contributes, if anything at all. We ask which of its inherited design choices benefit multimodal models trained entirely from scratch.

The predominant multimodal vision encoding recipes bundle together three design choices: (i) a visual prior from upstream pretraining, (ii) dedicated vision capacity (i.e., parameters that only vision tokens use), and (iii) pre-fusion placement of that capacity in a separate encoder that operates before vision and text tokens interact in the backbone—rather than operating in-fusion, within the shared backbone. A pretrained encoder keeps all three, a from-scratch encoder gives up only the prior, and an encoder-free model gives up all three.

Existing comparisons cannot isolate these choices, for two reasons. First, they entangle the choices with each other and the rest of the recipe. Published models differ in data, training stages, compute, and architecture. While controlled studies hold multimodal training data and compute fixed, their comparisons among pretrained encoders (McKinzie et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2024a; Fan et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) vary which visual prior an encoder imports rather than whether it needs one in the first place. Studies of encoder-based vs. encoder-free models either change all three choices (Tong et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026) or change capacity and placement together (Shukor et al., 2025). Second, comparisons with pretrained encoders control only multimodal training, treating encoder pretraining as free even though it adds substantial compute and data of its own (e.g., SigLIP 2 trains on 40B image–text samples; Tschannen et al., 2025), and several studies attribute the encoder’s advantage to its pretraining (Lei et al., 2025; Diao et al., 2025).

In this work, we conduct a controlled study that unbundles the design choices of multimodal vision encoding one at a time (fig. 1): (i) does the vision encoder need separate pretraining? (ii) does vision encoding need dedicated capacity? and (iii) does that capacity need to precede multimodal fusion? We train every model entirely from scratch, language backbone included, on a common pool of data with one encoder architecture, one dense backbone architecture, and one optimization recipe. We evaluate models on downstream visual question-answering (VQA) and language benchmarks at backbone sizes from 0.6B to 6.4B. Because recipes spend compute in different stages, we compare them at matched lifetime compute: the total compute of all training stages, including any pretraining of the encoder or language model.

Our experiments answer these questions and test whether the answers hold beyond lifetime compute:

  1. 1.

    Separate pretraining is optional (§3). At matched lifetime compute, a from-scratch encoder is on par with encoders pretrained on the same data. Even if we ignore upstream compute (§6.1), more encoder pretraining improves recognition but not VQA.

  2. 2.

    Dedicated vision capacity is key (§4). An encoder-free model trails an encoder-based model on visual understanding, even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder’s parameter count. The encoder’s advantage thus lies in capacity dedicated to vision rather than in total parameter count.

  3. 3.

    Vision capacity can move in-fusion (§5). Adding vision-only capacity to the backbone’s earliest layers is comparable to adding a from-scratch pre-fusion encoder. Scaling laws show in-fusion tracking the encoder, whereas encoder-free trails it at every size (§5.4).

  4. 4.

    The findings hold beyond lifetime compute (§6). Starting from a pretrained 1.7B language model, in-fusion stays comparable to the from-scratch encoder while encoder-free falls further behind. In-fusion can also lower time to first token, since no separate encoder must run before the backbone.

Together, these findings show that multimodal models benefit from dedicated vision capacity, which however needs neither separate pretraining nor pre-fusion placement.

2 A controlled protocol for comparing multimodal recipes

We propose a protocol that varies the three design choices a vision encoder bundles, while holding fixed the data sources, optimization settings, compute, and backbone architecture. This isolates their effects when comparing current multimodal model recipes. Conclusions about these design choices cannot be drawn from comparing published models, because they differ in several factors at once—e.g., they build on different pretrained language models and vision encoders that each vary in training data and compute. We therefore use no external pretrained models: we train every component from scratch, with common data sources and training setups, and compare recipes at matched lifetime compute, the total compute of all training stages.

2.1 Recipes and the fusion boundary

All recipes differ only in how they encode visual input.

Backbone.

Our backbones use an architecture modeled after Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025): a dense, decoder-only, pre-norm Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) with RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019), RoPE (Su et al., 2024), SwiGLU feed-forward layers (Shazeer, 2020), and grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) with query–key normalization (Dehghani et al., 2023) (section A.1). Our main comparisons (sections 3, 4 and 5) use the Qwen3 1.7B and 4B configurations with dedicated vision capacity fixed at 0.4B parameters, and our scaling study (section 5.4) uses a 0.6B–6.4B ladder that grows vision capacity in proportion to the backbone. Training uses autoregressive cross-entropy on text tokens; vision tokens precede the text they condition and have no loss. Each image’s vision tokens attend to each other bidirectionally and text tokens attend causally to all earlier tokens, including vision tokens (section A.4).

Fusion boundary.

We describe how image patches reach the backbone relative to the multimodal fusion boundary, the first layer in which vision and text tokens can interact: vision-only computation before it is pre-fusion and computation inside the shared backbone is in-fusion (figs. 1 and 1). Scratch encoders ( ) process image patches pre-fusion with a randomly initialized 27-layer, 0.4B-parameter Vision Transformer (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021; Alabdulmohsin et al., 2023) modeled after MoonViT-V2 (Kimi K3’s encoder; Kimi Team, 2026b), whose output is linearly projected into the backbone. Pretrained encoders ( ) share this architecture, but we first pretrain them ourselves on our common data (section 2.2) rather than taking external checkpoints. Encoder-free models ( ) map patches directly into the backbone with a linear patch embedding (Adept AI, 2023; Gemma Team, 2026), followed by RMSNorm and a learned scalar gate (Qi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). In-fusion models ( ) instead add vision-only modules inside the backbone (section 5). Every recipe trains on 224×224224\times 224 images, read as 256 vision tokens using 14×1414\times 14 patches. Instruction tuning for evaluation raises the resolution to 448×448448\times 448 (1,024 vision tokens), as in PaliGemma’s short high-resolution stage (Beyer et al., 2024), since OCR and chart reading needs fine detail (Tong et al., 2024a; Beyer, 2024).

2.2 Common data

Text-only sequences come from Nemotron-CC v2/v2.1 (NVIDIA, 2025b, a), and image–text sequences use MetaCLIP 1.2 pairs (English subset) (Xu et al., 2024). Encoder pretraining uses these pairs with their original alt-text, as in each objective’s original setup (section 3; e.g., CapPa, Tschannen et al., 2023), while multimodal training uses captions regenerated by Qwen2.5-VL-32B (Bai et al., 2025b) and shared by every recipe. Multimodal training mixes text-only and image–text sequences 70:30, so recipes with a pretrained encoder spend more lifetime compute on image–text data. This matches the language share Han et al. (2026) found optimal and gave the best visual understanding in our sweep at a small cost to text (section A.4).

2.3 Lifetime compute

Multimodal models often build on separately pretrained components whose training can even exceed the multimodal stage. For example, SigLIP 2, a commonly used encoder, is trained on 40B image–text samples (Tschannen et al., 2025), which translates to 10 trillion image tokens, while language models are typically also trained on trillions of text tokens (Touvron et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025). Counting only multimodal training therefore favors recipes that spend more compute in these earlier stages. To make such comparisons fair, we propose lifetime compute, the total training compute of every stage that produces the final model,

Clifetime=∑s∈𝒮Cs,C_{\mathrm{lifetime}}=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}C_{s}, (1)

where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the set of training stages and CsC_{s} is the training compute of stage ss. Here, 𝒮\mathcal{S} contains multimodal training, any text-only training before it and, for pretrained encoders, encoder pretraining, but not instruction tuning. We report compute in FLOPs; because recipes differ in cost per token, matched compute means that they process different numbers of tokens. Section A.5 describes the compute accounting and converts each budget into token-equivalents, the number of tokens a text-only model of the same size would process with the same compute. Lifetime compute models a project that allocates one budget across every training stage, which lets us separate the contribution of each design choice. In practice, pretrained encoders are often available for free, so we also compare encoders with their pretraining compute not counted (section 6.1).

2.4 Training schedule

To compare recipes at many training lengths from one run (Zhai et al., 2022), we use a warmup–stable–decay schedule (Hu et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2025; Hägele et al., 2024), where the learning rate stays constant after warmup and any checkpoint of that run can be decayed to 5% of its peak over the final 10% of training (section A.3). Our main comparisons span compute budgets from 6.5×10206.5\times 10^{20} to 2.9×10222.9\times 10^{22} FLOPs, or 56B to 1.11T token-equivalents (table 12). We index budgets by tokens per parameter (TPP): token-equivalents divided by the backbone’s non-embedding parameters, i.e., all parameters except the tied token embedding (1.4B at 1.7B and 3.6B at 4B; backbones are named by their total parameters). Budgets reach 788 TPP at 1.7B and 306 TPP at 4B. All recipes share one peak learning rate per backbone size, scaled with the inverse square root of its total parameter count (3×10−43\times 10^{-4} at 1.7B and 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} at 4B). At 1.7B, the encoder’s lead over encoder-free and parity with in-fusion hold from half to twice that learning rate (section F.2).

2.5 Evaluation

We evaluate recipes on text and visual understanding benchmarks and report the following metrics. Avg. Text averages four category means over 12 language benchmarks: commonsense reasoning (COPA, HellaSwag, PIQA, Social IQa, and WinoGrande (Roemmele et al., 2011; Zellers et al., 2019; Bisk et al., 2020; Sap et al., 2019; Sakaguchi et al., 2020)), science question answering (ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and OpenBookQA (Clark et al., 2018; Mihaylov et al., 2018)), broad knowledge (MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021)), and reading comprehension (RACE-middle, RACE-high, and BoolQ (Lai et al., 2017; Clark et al., 2019)). Avg. VQA averages the general, knowledge, OCR and chart, and vision-centric category means of the 16 Cambrian visual question-answering benchmarks (Tong et al., 2024a), after instruction tuning each checkpoint for three epochs on Cambrian-7M with 448×448448\times 448 images. A text-only model at the same lifetime compute serves as a reference for Avg. Text (section B.3). Sections 4 and 5.4 also compare held-out caption loss on images never seen in training (section B.4). Appendix B details the benchmarks, and appendix I gives every benchmark score.

3 Does the vision encoder need separate pretraining?

The first design choice a vision encoder bundles is a visual prior imported through separate pretraining, which recent models (Kimi Team, 2026b) forgo by training the encoder from scratch with the language model. Under a fixed lifetime compute budget, encoder pretraining directly competes with multimodal training for FLOPs. Whether the prior is needed also shapes the remainder of our study, because encoder-free architectures cannot easily import one. We test whether the prior helps by comparing encoders pretrained with different objectives against the same encoder trained from scratch with the backbone.

Setup.

We pretrain a separate encoder with each of four objectives and the same compute: contrastive image–text alignment (MetaCLIP; Xu et al., 2024), self-supervised learning (WebSSL; Fan et al., 2025), and captioning (Cap and CapPa; Tschannen et al., 2023). Pretrained encoders are updated during multimodal training and compared with an encoder trained from scratch at matched lifetime compute; we also test a frozen MetaCLIP encoder. MetaCLIP, an instance of widely used CLIP-style pretraining (Radford et al., 2021; Zhai et al., 2023; Tschannen et al., 2025), serves as the pretrained reference in the remaining experiments. Section C.1 details the pretraining objectives and section A.1 the encoder architecture.

A from-scratch encoder is on par with pretrained ones.

With a 1.7B backbone and a 1.04×10221.04\times 10^{22} FLOP budget, all four pretrained encoders are comparable to the from-scratch encoder when pretraining takes 7.4% or 15% of the budget (e.g., Cap sees 1B or 2B image–text examples). Larger upstream shares hurt multimodal performance: at a 60% share, both averages fall clearly below the from-scratch encoder (fig. 2). Across backbone sizes, the from-scratch encoder matches or exceeds MetaCLIP at every budget (fig. 2). Appendix C gives the per-objective results, including frozen encoders, the full pretraining sweep, the results at 4B, and compositional image–text matching on SugarCrepe (Hsieh et al., 2023).

Encoder pretraining does not help even when its compute is free (section 6.1). More pretraining raises ImageNet accuracy but not Avg. VQA, and pretrained encoders are only comparable to the from-scratch encoder at matched multimodal compute. Delaying vision also hurts, as training on text alone for the first 25–75% of training, with the total number of image–text examples held fixed, clearly lowers Avg. VQA (table 11), consistent with the vision laziness that Han et al. (2026) observe after text-only training.

Takeaway 1: Encoder pretraining offers little advantage. At matched lifetime compute, an encoder trained from scratch together with the backbone is on par with encoders pretrained on the same data.

4 Does vision encoding need dedicated capacity?

The from-scratch encoder of section 3 forgoes the imported prior but keeps the second design choice: dedicated vision capacity. Encoder-free models drop this capacity entirely and project image patches directly into the shared backbone (Adept AI, 2023; Diao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026; Gemma Team, 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a). Dropping the encoder, however, also removes a substantial number of parameters and changes how raw patches enter the backbone, so a gap between the two recipes could reflect fewer total parameters, a weak patch embedding, or missing dedicated capacity. In this section, we test whether visual understanding needs this dedicated capacity, leaving the study of its precise placement to section 5.

Setup.

We compare the from-scratch encoder (section 3) with the encoder-free recipe (section 2.1), which maps each patch into the backbone with a linear patch embedding followed by RMSNorm and a learned gate. As in every recipe, vision tokens attend to one another bidirectionally in the backbone (section 2.1). Both recipes share common backbones, data, and lifetime compute budgets, and we compare them at 1.7B and 4B.

Encoder-free trails encoder on visual understanding.

Figure 3 shows that Avg. VQA clearly suffers from a missing encoder, across scales and budgets, while Avg. Text stays comparable. This also holds when scaling the encoder’s size (section 5.4). This result differs from Shukor et al. (2025), who find that encoder-free models match or slightly outperform encoder-based ones, mainly at smaller sizes. We identify two choices in their setup that work against the encoder (section D.4). First, their encoder’s learning rate may have been too small. Second, they fit their scaling laws to an average of text, interleaved, and caption losses, which drowns out the signal from vision. In-distribution held-out caption loss instead shows the encoder-free deficit and tracks Avg. VQA across recipes, sizes, and budgets (fig. 18), whereas their averaged loss hides it.

Matching total parameters does not overcome encoder-free’s deficit.

We next widen or deepen the encoder-free backbone by 0.4B parameters to match the vision parameters added by the encoder (table 2; 4B in table 19). None of the variants comes close to closing the gap on Avg. VQA, though all improve Avg. Text, since text tokens also use the added parameters. The remaining gap in visual understanding is largest on OCR and chart benchmarks. The same parameters are thus more useful as a vision encoder. As none of these variants improves Avg. VQA, encoder-free hereafter keeps the plain backbone shared across all recipes.

A richer patch embedding does not close the gap.

We also study replacing the encoder-free linear patch embedding with two richer ones: a normalized two-layer projection inspired by Gemma 4 (Gemma Team, 2026), and a four-layer hierarchical MLP (Touvron et al., 2022), as in Inkling (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a). Trained on 224×224224\times 224 images, neither comes close to the encoder (table 2), though the hierarchical MLP matches it when compressing 640×640640\times 640 images into the same 256 tokens (section D.3). Subsequent encoder-free experiments keep the default patch embedding, so dedicated capacity is placed deliberately.

Takeaway 2: Visual understanding benefits from dedicated vision capacity. Encoder-free models trail the from-scratch encoder on Avg. VQA. Adding backbone capacity with the same encoder parameter budget does not close the gap.

5 Does dedicated capacity need to precede multimodal fusion?

Section 4 shows that visual understanding benefits from dedicated capacity. We now ask whether that capacity must precede multimodal fusion. The encoder’s parameters are both dedicated, used only by vision tokens, and pre-fusion, processing vision tokens before they interact with text. We test whether pre-fusion placement is needed by moving the encoder’s parameter budget in-fusion, into vision-only modules inside the shared backbone (section 5.1). Section 5.2 studies where this capacity should sit, which tokens should use it, and which modules it adds. Sections 5.3 and 5.4 then compare it with the encoder over training and with scale.

5.1 Moving the encoder’s capacity inside the backbone

In-fusion vision capacity adds vision-only modules to selected backbone layers. In each of these layers, the attention projections and the feed-forward network (FFN) keep their shared weights and add vision-only counterparts, whose outputs add to the shared outputs after each module (fig. 4). Each vision-only module thus acts as an additive expert routed by modality: vision tokens use it alongside the shared weights. Unlike mixture-of-transformers (MoT; Liang et al., 2025), which gives text and vision tokens entirely separate parameters, in-fusion still passes every token through the shared parameters. Section 6.2 compares the two when starting from pretrained language models.

For token ii with vision indicator mi∈{0,1}m_{i}\in\{0,1\}, each attention projection WPW_{P} gains a vision-only counterpart Δ​WP\Delta W_{P} that applies only to vision tokens,

P​(𝐳i)=WP​𝐳i+mi​Δ​WP​𝐳i,P∈{Q,K,V,O},P(\mathbf{z}_{i})=W_{P}\,\mathbf{z}_{i}+m_{i}\,\Delta W_{P}\,\mathbf{z}_{i},\qquad P\in\{Q,K,V,O\}, (2)

where 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i} is the projection’s input (the normalized hidden state for QQ, KK, VV and the attention output for OO). Attention thus remains joint across vision and text tokens. The FFN gains a vision-only branch,

𝐡i′=𝐡i+F​(N​(𝐡i))+mi​Δ​F​(N​(𝐡i)),\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\prime}=\mathbf{h}_{i}+F\!\left(N(\mathbf{h}_{i})\right)+m_{i}\,\Delta F\!\left(N(\mathbf{h}_{i})\right), (3)

where FF is the shared FFN, NN is its normalization, and Δ​F\Delta F is a vision-only FFN of the same form that reads the same normalized input (section E.1). The vision-only projections Δ​WP\Delta W_{P} and the output projection of Δ​F\Delta F are zero-initialized, so training starts from the shared model. Because these modules act only when mi=1m_{i}=1, text-only inputs are processed exactly as they would have been by the shared backbone.

We use two variants: “in-fusion”, our default, adds vision FFN branches of smaller hidden width and vision-only counterparts of all four attention projections, while “in-fusion (FFN-only)” adds only vision FFN branches. We size both variants to match the encoder’s vision-only parameter budget (table 23), so comparisons with the encoder vary only where dedicated capacity is placed. Existing vision-specific architectures do not fit this comparison: they either duplicate vision weights that scale with the backbone (Wang et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2025) or use vision adapters that rely on an encoder (Dong et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025).

5.2 Where and how to add in-fusion capacity

We compare in-fusion designs that reallocate the encoder’s 0.4B vision parameters within the backbone.

Placement of capacity within fusion.

We study placement with the FFN-only variant, because FFN branches can be narrowed to fit any placement. Full-rank vision-only attention projections cannot, because adding them to every layer would take 88% of the 0.4B budget at 1.7B and exceed it at 4B. With the budget fixed, we compare four placements (table 3): a narrow branch in every layer, or eight wider branches spread evenly across depth, in the last eight layers, or in the first eight layers. The first three variants do no better than the encoder-free model on Avg. VQA, whereas placing the modules in the first eight layers matches the scratch encoder. Early placement also helps most on OCR and chart questions, which depend on fine visual detail, whereas late placement does not. Dedicated in-fusion capacity is therefore most useful where the backbone first processes vision tokens, similar to an encoder. We hypothesize that vision tokens benefit most from vision-only processing while they are still close to raw patch features. Only early placement concentrates the budget there, whereas the every-layer and spread placements dilute it across the backbone. Layerwise representation similarity shows that the in-fusion models change vision tokens mostly within the first eight blocks, where their vision-only modules sit, and little afterward, while the encoder-free model keeps changing them through shared blocks 4–13 (section E.4). Therefore, we use the first eight layers from here on.

Reserving the capacity for vision tokens matters.

To check that the gain comes from reserving this capacity for vision tokens, we also give the same parameters in the first eight layers to all tokens (table 3). Widening the shared FFNs barely improves over the encoder-free model. A separate branch used by all tokens recovers some of the vision-only branch’s gain, but still trails it even with twice the training (table 24). The all-token variants slightly improve on Avg. Text, because text also uses the added parameters. We hypothesize that a vision-only branch gives vision tokens processing of their own without competing with text for the same parameters, while both still share the backbone’s attention and FFNs.

Adding vision-only attention projections.

With the capacity confined to the first eight layers, the QKVO attention projections fit within the budget (0.1B at 1.7B), so “in-fusion” adds them alongside narrower FFN branches. It is comparable to FFN-only at 1.7B and slightly ahead at every 4B budget (fig. 5), and its vision-only attention projections help on their own at 4B (section E.2), so we use this variant as our default for the remainder of the paper.

5.3 Can in-fusion capacity match a pre-fusion encoder?

With the same dedicated budget on either side of the multimodal fusion boundary, we compare in-fusion with a scratch encoder at matched lifetime compute over training at 1.7B and 4B (fig. 6). In-fusion is comparable to the encoder throughout. Like the encoder, in-fusion clearly leads encoder-free at both sizes; section 5.4 compares the recipes across backbone sizes. Part of the in-fusion budget sits in vision-only attention projections, which help on their own in additional 4B ablations (section E.2). Dedicated vision capacity therefore does not need to precede fusion to benefit visual understanding. In-fusion can also lower time to first token for image requests, since no encoder runs before the backbone (section 6.3).

5.4 Results hold with scale

So far, we have compared the recipes at 1.7B and 4B with 0.4B of dedicated vision capacity. To see how they behave with scale, we train them on a ladder of five backbone sizes from 0.6B to 6.4B (setup in appendix G). The dedicated vision capacity grows with the backbone, keeping its share of parameters from the 1.7B model, as in jointly scaled models (Chen et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2025). For each recipe, we fit Avg. VQA, caption loss, and text loss as functions of model size NN and token-equivalents DD on all of its ladder runs. At every size, encoder-free needs approximately three times the encoder’s compute to match it on Avg. VQA and caption loss, while in-fusion tracks the encoder (fig. 7). On text loss and Avg. Text, the three recipes are comparable (tables 30 and 29). Taken together, the findings of sections 4 and 5 hold with scale.

Takeaway 3: Dedicated vision capacity can move into the backbone’s earliest layers. Placed in the earliest layers, vision-only modules with the encoder’s budget are comparable to a from-scratch encoder at every backbone size.

6 Vision encoding beyond lifetime compute

Our main investigations (sections 3, 4 and 5) are deliberately controlled: they train every component from scratch and charge each stage’s compute to one lifetime budget, which enables us to isolate the three design choices of a vision encoder. In practice, however, multimodal models are often built from separately pretrained components: a language model and, usually, a vision encoder. Inference speed for serving also shapes these design decisions. We find that a “free” pretrained encoder still does not help a backbone trained from scratch (section 6.1), and that instead midtraining a 1.7B text-only model leaves the comparisons of sections 3, 4 and 5 unchanged (section 6.2). Finally, in-fusion can lower the time to first token for image requests (section 6.3).

6.1 Zero-cost pretrained encoders

Section 3 charges encoder pretraining to the lifetime budget, but in practice a pretrained encoder is often available for free. Here, we hold multimodal training fixed at 2.7×10212.7\times 10^{21} FLOPs and vary MetaCLIP pretraining from 1.4×10211.4\times 10^{21} to 9.0×10219.0\times 10^{21} FLOPs. This raises the encoder’s ImageNet linear-probe accuracy before multimodal training from 80.4% to 84.4% (fig. 9; section C.3), yet Avg. VQA is highest after the shortest pretraining, and an encoder trained from scratch with the same multimodal training matches it. Thus, even when pretraining is free, more of it does not help.

6.2 Midtraining from pretrained language models

Many multimodal models add vision to a language model pretrained on text alone (Alayrac et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2024a; Bai et al., 2025a). We call this stage of continued training on multimodal data midtraining. We test whether the comparisons of sections 3, 4 and 5 hold in this setting. We pretrain our own 1.7B language model on 1T tokens of the same text data and then midtrain it to 1.33T token-equivalents with each recipe at equal compute (fig. 9). Following DeepSeek-VL (Lu et al., 2024a), midtraining keeps 70% text data; as in section 6.1, MetaCLIP’s encoder pretraining is not counted. Besides the four recipes, we compare MoT (section 5.1, initialized from the language model) and a variant that copies only its first eight layers, matching the encoder’s 0.4B vision-only parameters.

In-fusion, MoT layers 1–8, and the from-scratch encoder perform comparably, and all lead encoder-free. The full MoT model falls behind despite 3.5 times as many vision-only parameters—adding vision-only copies of the later layers to MoT layers 1–8 hurts, consistent with late placement not helping in section 5.2. A free MetaCLIP encoder, which matches the from-scratch encoder when the backbone is also trained from scratch (section 6.1), trails it here, mostly on OCR, chart, and vision-centric questions. Tuning each encoder’s learning rate does not change these conclusions (section H.1). We hypothesize that the from-scratch encoder learns features suited to the pretrained language model from its first update, whereas MetaCLIP’s contrastive features, which miss fine visual detail (Tong et al., 2024b), must be reshaped by a language model that already leans on text. Every recipe keeps Avg. Text within a point of a text-only control. Thus, the conclusions from our controlled experiments (sections 3, 4 and 5) carry over to midtraining, where a free pretrained encoder trails the from-scratch encoder, encoder-free trails on VQA, and in-fusion is comparable to the pre-fusion encoder.

6.3 Training and inference speed

A separate encoder must finish processing each image before the backbone can start, which adds a serial step to inference. Following the inference benchmark of Mono-InternVL (Luo et al., 2025b), we measure time to first token (TTFT) on one H200 with 16 concurrent requests, each with one 448-pixel image and 256 text tokens (section H.3). At 1.7B with 0.4B vision-only parameters, in-fusion and its FFN-only variant are clearly faster than the encoder (fig. 10) at comparable Avg. VQA (table 26). MoT, which copies the first kk backbone layers for vision tokens, is about as fast as in-fusion up to 0.4B vision-only parameters, but its added TTFT grows faster with the budget, while staying below the encoder’s TTFT. Encoder-free is fastest but clearly trails on Avg. VQA (table 26). In-fusion’s TTFT advantage over the encoder grows with the vision-only budget (fig. 10), which scales with the backbone (section 5.4); at a fixed budget, vision adds nearly the same time at 1.7B and 4B (table 36). Earlier encoder-free models report larger TTFT reductions, up to 69% (Luo et al., 2025b, a), although their gains also reflect other efficiency changes. Inference benefits also depend on deployment details. Under continuous batching of mixed text and image requests, in-fusion’s vision-only modules run in the same forward passes as text-only requests, whereas a separate encoder adds latency only to image requests. Finally, both in-fusion variants train as fast as encoder-free, whereas the encoder recipe is 3% slower at 4B (table 35).

Takeaway 4: Our findings hold beyond lifetime compute, and in-fusion can be faster to serve. A free pretrained encoder still does not help, the comparisons carry over to midtraining, and in-fusion lowers TTFT at comparable VQA.

7 Related work

Multimodal model recipes.

Most multimodal models connect a separately pretrained vision encoder (Radford et al., 2021; Tschannen et al., 2025; Bolya et al., 2025), kept frozen (Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023b; Muse Glimmer Team, 2026) or updated (Beyer et al., 2024; Steiner et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025a), to a pretrained language model. More recent models train the encoder from scratch with the language model (Kimi Team, 2026b; Tian et al., 2025), embed image patches without an encoder (Adept AI, 2023; Diao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Gemma Team, 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a), or quantize images with a separately trained tokenizer (Chameleon Team, 2024; Wang et al., 2026). Inkling was released as “encoder-free”, yet its successor, Inkling 2 Small, uses a 292M-parameter vision encoder (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a, b). Because these models also differ in data, pretrained components, and compute, comparing them directly does not isolate a single design choice. We therefore train every stage of each recipe class from scratch on common data sources and compare the recipes at matched lifetime compute (section 2).

Controlled studies.

Prior controlled studies of encoder pretraining typically start from a pretrained language model, count only multimodal training, and compare encoder pretraining objectives and data (Karamcheti et al., 2024; McKinzie et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2024a; Laurençon et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) rather than studying whether separate pretraining is needed at all. The few works that compare pretrained and from-scratch encoders vary in their findings, possibly because they control neither the encoder’s pretraining data nor lifetime compute (Tian et al., 2025; Kimi Team, 2026b). Studies raise a similar question for language pretraining, finding that adding vision before text-only pretraining ends, rather than after it, improves visual understanding (Keh et al., 2025; Han et al., 2026; Kimi Team, 2026a), as in our delayed-vision experiments (table 11). Encoder pretraining also confounds encoder vs. encoder-free comparisons, which typically pit a pretrained encoder against an encoder-free model (Beyer et al., 2024; Diao et al., 2024; Lei et al., 2025; Diao et al., 2025; Tong et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). Such comparisons remove separate pretraining, dedicated capacity, and pre-fusion placement at once, and often attribute the encoder’s advantage to pretraining data they do not control. Shukor et al. (2025), who train both designs from scratch, find that encoder-free models match or slightly outperform an encoder. In contrast, we find that the encoder leads on VQA and held-out caption loss, which we trace to their setup (section D.4).

Dedicated vision capacity.

Testing whether dedicated capacity must precede fusion requires moving the encoder’s capacity inside the backbone, which the encoder vs. encoder-free comparisons cannot accomplish. Prior works on fusion depth come closer, varying where modalities begin to interact (Nagrani et al., 2021; Hao et al., 2026) or where encoder features enter the backbone (Meng et al., 2024), but none moves a fixed amount of vision-only capacity into layers that vision and text share. Other multimodal architectures add vision-specific parameters to the backbone, but not in a form that fits this comparison. Modality-expert designs duplicate the backbone’s weights for vision tokens, typically in every layer, and route vision tokens through these copies instead of the shared weights (Bao et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2025). Their vision-only capacity is thus set by the backbone’s size and spread over its depth rather than held at an encoder’s budget early in the model, and most also build on a pretrained language model (Wang et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025b; Tian et al., 2025; Diao et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025). Adapter architectures fine-tune a pretrained model through small parallel or low-rank modules shared by all tokens (He et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2022), and their multimodal variants keep an encoder alongside the adapters (Dong et al., 2024; Shapourian et al., 2026) or distill from one (Wang et al., 2025). The encoders in these works still supply pre-fusion capacity or a pretrained prior, the two factors our comparison aims to remove. We instead give vision tokens their own attention projections and feed-forward branches in selected backbone layers. Their outputs add to the shared ones and together match an encoder’s parameter budget, so only the placement of this capacity changes (section 5). Placed in the first eight layers, in-fusion capacity is comparable to a pre-fusion encoder on VQA, so dedicated vision capacity helps whether it sits pre-fusion or in-fusion.

8 Discussion

With multimodal models revisiting the vision encoder, we asked which of its design choices are still beneficial. We proposed unbundling the encoder into three choices: a visual prior from separate pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity. We tested each by training every recipe from scratch on common data, with one architecture and optimization setup, and comparing recipes on text and visual understanding benchmarks at matched lifetime compute.

Takeaways from unbundling.

Of the three choices an encoder bundles, only dedicated vision capacity maintains its advantage. Separate pretraining is unnecessary: an encoder trained jointly with the backbone is on par with pretrained ones, and longer pretraining improves recognition but not VQA, even when it is free (sections 3 and 6.1). Dedicated capacity matters: with the encoder’s parameters added to their shared backbone, encoder-free models gain on Avg. Text but still trail the encoder on Avg. VQA (section 4), most on OCR and chart questions (table 2). This capacity belongs early, but it need not precede the backbone: vision-only modules in the first backbone layers are comparable to a pre-fusion encoder (section 5). For recipes that drop the encoder, this suggests reallocating its parameters as vision-only capacity in the earliest layers rather than as shared parameters.

Limitations and future work.

To keep comparisons controlled, we pretrain encoders on the same images as multimodal training, so our results do not rule out a benefit from released encoders trained on additional data. Encoder pretraining uses the images’ original alt-text, as in standard image–text pretraining; pretraining on our regenerated captions instead changes little (table 9). Our experiments are on dense backbones with up to 6.4B parameters; the most compelling next step is extending them to sparse mixture-of-experts backbones, whose experts could naturally host in-fusion’s modality-routed capacity. Multimodal training also uses 224×224224\times 224 MetaCLIP images, leaving higher-resolution training and more text-rich data to future work. The text–image data mixture was selected with the from-scratch encoder at 1.7B, so mixtures tuned for each recipe remain underexplored (section A.4). Finally, how architecture interacts with interleaved image–text and video data remains open.

Conclusion.

We presented a controlled study that disentangles the design choices behind how multimodal models process visual input, studying each choice in isolation instead of as part of a bundled recipe. Rather than assembling multimodal models from components optimized for different objectives, our findings favor training them end-to-end as one system.

Appendix A Controlled protocol

Unless stated otherwise, every comparison of the 1.7B and 4B backbones uses the settings below, which detail the protocol of section 2.

A.1 Architectures

The multimodal recipes differ in where their vision-only capacity sits and how it is trained: in a pre-fusion vision encoder that is pretrained and then frozen or updated, or trained from scratch, encoder-free with no module besides a patch embedding, or vision-only modules inside the shared backbone (in-fusion vision capacity; section E.1). Unless a variable is the stated ablation, comparisons hold the backbone, the 256 vision tokens per image in multimodal training, the data, the optimization recipe, and lifetime compute fixed. Table 4 lists the backbone and encoder architectures.

Backbone.

The shared backbone is a dense decoder-only Transformer that follows the Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B configurations (Yang et al., 2025) and is trained from random initialization. Its FFNs use SwiGLU (Shazeer, 2020), and its attention uses grouped key–value heads with RMSNorm on queries and keys. The vision-only FFN branches of in-fusion vision capacity use the same form and read the same normalized input as the shared FFN (section E.1).

Vision encoder.

The encoder follows MoonViT-V2, the vision encoder of Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026b), in depth, patch size, normalization, and size: 27 layers, patch size 14, RMSNorm, and about 0.4B parameters in total. It has width 1,024 with 4,096-wide MLPs and uses learned spatial position embeddings combined with interleaved two-dimensional rotary position embeddings. During multimodal training, each image is resized bilinearly to a shorter side of 224 pixels, center-cropped to 224×224224\times 224, and divided into 14×1414\times 14 patches, producing 256 vision tokens. For an image xx, the encoder recipe computes

venc​(x)=Wproj​fϕ​(x),v_{\mathrm{enc}}(x)=W_{\mathrm{proj}}f_{\phi}(x), (4)

where fϕf_{\phi} is the vision encoder and the linear projector WprojW_{\mathrm{proj}} maps its output width to the backbone width. Pretrained variants (section 3) use the same architecture and differ only in the pretraining objective. MetaCLIP and WebSSL use a class token during upstream training; we discard it and pass only the 256 patch tokens to the backbone (Liu et al., 2023).

Encoder-free patch embedding.

The encoder-free recipe projects each flattened 14×1414\times 14 RGB patch linearly into the backbone width, as in Fuyu and Gemma 4 (Adept AI, 2023; Gemma Team, 2026), and applies RMSNorm and a learned scalar gate (Qi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026), giving 256 backbone tokens per image:

where p2​Dp_{2\mathrm{D}} is a fixed two-dimensional sine–cosine position embedding and the learned scalar gate gg is initialized to 0.10.1. The in-fusion models of section E.1 use the same patch embedding.

We chose the from-scratch encoder’s shape and size at matched lifetime compute, and every main comparison uses the resulting 27-layer, 0.4B encoder. The shape and size comparisons use the 1.7B backbone at 2.6×10212.6\times 10^{21} FLOPs (table 5).

The configurations in table 5 vary the structure of the dedicated visual computation. Half-Depth, Wide, and Shallow + Wide are pre-fusion encoders that change the default encoder’s depth, width, or both. The backbone-style encoder is also a pre-fusion encoder. It has its own patch embedding and eight Transformer blocks shaped like those of the 1.7B backbone, and it connects to the backbone through the linear projection of eq. 4. The Default, Shallow + Wide, and backbone-style variants use about the same vision-only parameter budget; the Half-Depth and Wide variants test smaller and larger budgets, respectively. The “Size” section of table 5 scales the default encoder’s depth and width together, from Small (0.05B) to Huge (0.92B). At matched lifetime compute, encoders with more parameters process fewer tokens.

The default encoder is comparable to Wide on VQA while using fewer vision-only parameters. Avg. Text does not follow encoder size: Small and Huge score highest, and the default slightly lower.

At 4B.

We further ablate encoder size at the 4B model scale, using the same from-scratch recipe (table 6). The default Large encoder is strongest on both Avg. Text and Avg. VQA. At both scales, the default encoder gives the highest Avg. VQA, and Avg. Text does not follow encoder size.

At 6.4B.

On the 6.4B backbone of the size ladder (appendix G), we also keep the 0.4B encoder instead of scaling it to 1.7B with the backbone. It is comparable to the scaled encoder on both averages at every budget (table 7), so the default encoder does not limit the encoder recipe at larger backbones either.

A.3 Optimization settings

Table 8 lists the optimization settings for multimodal training and instruction tuning. We train the Transformer weight matrices with Muon (Jordan et al., 2024), applied per head to the query, key, and value projections (Kimi Team, 2026b), and the embeddings, output heads, normalization parameters, and biases with AdamW. The peak learning rate scales with the inverse square root of the backbone’s total parameter count, and training follows a warmup–stable–decay schedule (Hu et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2025; Hägele et al., 2024). Checkpoints taken before the final decay use a constant learning rate. The decay lowers the learning rate linearly to 5% of its peak over the last 10% of updates, so a run whose stable phase ends at compute CC finishes at C/0.9C/0.9 (for example, 1.17×10221.17\times 10^{22} and 1.30×10221.30\times 10^{22} FLOPs at 1.7B and 2.61×10222.61\times 10^{22} and 2.90×10222.90\times 10^{22} FLOPs at 4B; table 12).

A.4 Training data and mixture

Text-only sequences come from Nemotron-CC v2 (NVIDIA, 2025b) and v2.1 (NVIDIA, 2025a), and image–text sequences use MetaCLIP 1.2 image–text pairs (English subset) (Xu et al., 2024). Every training sequence has 4,096 tokens and packs several documents. Attention is bidirectional among the vision tokens of each image and causal otherwise. It stays within each document in image–text sequences and in every sequence of the text-only reference, whereas the text sequences of image-trained models attend across packed documents. Multimodal training uses a 70:30 mixture of text and image–text sequences, which we select below (table 10). Each image is processed at 224×224224\times 224 resolution and yields 256 vision tokens (section A.1). An image–text sequence packs about 12.8 MetaCLIP 1.2 pairs, each one image and its caption, so vision tokens fill about 80% of an image–text sequence and, under the 70:30 mixture, about 24% of all training tokens. Below, the data ablation varies the mixture and the study of when image–text data enters training uses a 90:10 mixture; the richer patch embeddings of section D.3 read higher-resolution images.

Recaptioning.

Multimodal training uses captions regenerated once for the MetaCLIP 1.2 images by Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025b) and shared by every recipe, while encoder pretraining uses the original alt-text (section 2). We use nucleus sampling with temperature 0.6 and top-pp 0.95, generating at most 128 new tokens. The system prompt is:

You are an expert image captioner. Write one specific, information-dense caption (1–2 sentences). Do not begin with 'A', 'An', or 'The'. Name the main subject first, then key objects, attributes, actions, and scene context. Avoid hedging and meta phrases.

The user prompt is:

Generate a caption for this image.

Caption source for encoder pretraining.

To ablate the choice of regenerated captions versus alt-text, we pretrain the CapPa encoder for 7.7×10207.7\times 10^{20} FLOPs on either the alt-text or our regenerated captions and train it with the 1B ladder backbone (table 28), a 0.4B encoder, and the 70:30 mixture, against the from-scratch encoder, to 32 and 64 tokens per parameter (table 9). The regenerated-caption encoder scores slightly higher Avg. VQA than the alt-text encoder and matches the from-scratch encoder.

Data mixture.

We select the 70:30 mixture of text and image–text sequences by an ablation on the 1.7B backbone with a from-scratch vision encoder, consistent with controlled studies of data balance in early multimodal training (Han et al., 2026). At the same lifetime compute (2.34×10212.34\times 10^{21} FLOPs, at a constant learning rate), we compare it with 100:0, 90:10, and 50:50 mixtures (table 10). The 70:30 mixture gives the best Avg. VQA with slight degradation to text, whereas 90:10 keeps Avg. Text closer to the text-only model.

We use 70:30 for the main comparisons as it gives a strong balance of visual understanding and language ability.

When image–text data enters.

We also vary the point in training at which image–text data enters. Every schedule allocates 10% of lifetime training examples to image–text data, a 90:10 mixture rather than the constant 70:30 mixture above. We compare schedules that begin image–text training at different points while keeping the total number of image–text examples and lifetime compute fixed (fig. 11). Later schedules continue the language model and optimizer, add a randomly initialized vision encoder and projector, and warm up the new parameters for 4,000 updates. Starting image–text training at the first update gives the strongest visual understanding. Starting at 25%, 50%, or 75% of training lowers Avg. VQA, with the largest drops on general and on OCR and chart questions, while Avg. Text stays comparable (table 11).

A.5 Compute accounting

Lifetime compute (eq. 1) sums the training compute of every stage that produces the final model: multimodal training for every recipe, encoder pretraining for pretrained encoders, and, in midtraining (section 6.2), the text-only pretraining of the language model. As with fine-tuning in transfer evaluation, instruction tuning is a fixed downstream step applied to every checkpoint to measure VQA (appendix B), so it is not counted. Each term uses the same algorithmic count of forward- and backward-pass matrix multiplication and convolution FLOPs for the modules active in that stage (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). The count excludes activation recomputation (Chowdhery et al., 2023), optimizer updates, communication, elementwise operations, and input processing. A frozen encoder receives no backward pass during multimodal training, so it is charged only its forward pass, one third of its training cost. The free-encoder comparison of section 6.1 instead matches multimodal training compute and does not charge encoder pretraining.

Charging pretrained checkpoints.

A pretrained encoder is charged the full compute of its upstream training up to the checkpoint used. Because a MetaCLIP example costs less compute than a captioning example, the same upstream compute buys MetaCLIP about 12% more epochs. The objective comparisons hold upstream compute equal across objectives, so they use MetaCLIP checkpoints matched to the compute of 1, 2, 4, and 8 captioning epochs (section C.1). The sweep of section C.3 compares MetaCLIP only with itself, so it uses MetaCLIP’s own 2-, 4-, 8-, and 13-epoch checkpoints.

Token-equivalent budgets.

To provide intuition about compute scales, we also express each budget in token-equivalents, the number of tokens that a text-only model of the same backbone size would train on with the same compute:

Heq=ClifetimecLM,H_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{lifetime}}}{c_{\mathrm{LM}}}, (6)

where cLMc_{\mathrm{LM}} is that text-only model’s training FLOPs per token, 1.17×10101.17\times 10^{10} at 1.7B and 2.61×10102.61\times 10^{10} at 4B. For example, a budget of 200B token-equivalents is 2.34×10212.34\times 10^{21} FLOPs at 1.7B, and table 12 gives every decayed budget in FLOPs and tokens per parameter; a constant-learning-rate checkpoint sits at 0.9 times its decayed budget (section A.3).

Architecture and data mixture change the number of updates at fixed compute. For instance, at 2.34×10212.34\times 10^{21} FLOPs, the 1.7B text-only model takes 47.7K updates of 1,024×4,0961{,}024\times 4{,}096 tokens (200B tokens), and the from-scratch encoder recipe with the 70:30 mixture takes 45.3K, because the encoder’s computation also counts toward the budget.

Appendix B Evaluation

This section describes the two main evaluation metrics, Avg. VQA and Avg. Text. We also define the held-out losses that sections 4, 5.4 and F.3 use as well as two additional metrics, out-of-distribution caption loss and ImageNet linear-probe accuracy.

B.1 VQA benchmarks

Visual instruction tuning.

We use instruction tuning as an evaluation protocol (Tong et al., 2024a). Every multimodal model checkpoint is instruction-tuned with one fixed recipe before we measure its visual understanding. The recipe runs three epochs of Cambrian-7M (Tong et al., 2024a) before evaluation. Multimodal training reads 224×224224\times 224 images, but instruction tuning and evaluation raise the resolution to 448×448448\times 448 (1,024 vision tokens), since OCR and chart reading needs fine detail (Tong et al., 2024a; Beyer, 2024). Exhibits whose captions say so instead retain the multimodal-training resolution of 224×224224\times 224 (256 vision tokens), otherwise with the same recipe. The encoder’s learned position table is interpolated to the larger patch grid, and the fixed sine–cosine positions of encoder-free and in-fusion models are recomputed for it. Cambrian-7M is a curated instruction-tuning mixture spanning general visual tasks, OCR and charts, counting, math, science, code, and language-only data. Table 8 provides the optimizer settings and batch size. Instruction tuning updates the same parameters as multimodal training. Therefore, a frozen encoder, e.g., the frozen MetaCLIP encoder in table 16, stays frozen.

Benchmarks and Avg. VQA.

Evaluation follows the Cambrian-1 visual understanding suite (Tong et al., 2024a), using greedy decoding with at most 256 output tokens. Each task is capped at its first 5,000 examples in dataset order. Table 13 lists the 16 benchmarks in four categories (general, knowledge, OCR and chart, and vision-centric), with the split, metric, and number of examples for each. Exact match compares the normalized parsed answer or option letter with the reference answers, relaxed accuracy tolerates small numeric errors, and VQA accuracy is the consensus metric (Antol et al., 2015) that TextVQA uses. Each category mean averages its four benchmarks. The suite contains 15 benchmarks scored in [0,100][0,100] and MME-Perception (MME-P), whose ten subtasks each score out of 200. We divide the MME-P total by 20 to put it on the same scale, and Avg. VQA is the mean of the 16 scores, which equals the mean of the four category means.

Blank-image control.

The blank-image control separates visual understanding from what the question alone supports. It replaces every image with zeros during both instruction tuning and evaluation while keeping the vision-token positions. We use it only for the text-only (100:0) row of the data-mixture ablation (table 10), which has no trained visual pathway. At 1.7B, this row reaches 28 Avg. VQA, a measure of how much the questions alone support (Goyal et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2026).

B.2 Language benchmarks

Language evaluations use the multimodal checkpoint without instruction tuning. Table 14 lists the 12 benchmarks, their categories, and how each is scored. All tasks rank the answer choices by log-likelihood; MMLU uses five subject-matched demonstrations and averages its 57 subjects equally, and the other tasks are zero-shot. Avg. Text is the mean of the four category scores, each the mean of its benchmarks, with ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge averaged into one ARC score and RACE-middle and RACE-high combined by test-question count.

B.3 Text-only reference

At the same text-token budget, the multimodal recipes score about as well on Avg. Text as a text-only reference trained on the same text: on average 0.1 point below it at 1.7B and 0.6 below at 4B (fig. 12). The encoder, encoder-free, and in-fusion recipes behave alike. At matched lifetime compute, the reference leads by 0.5 to 3.9 points (table 27), because multimodal training gives 30% of its sequences to image–text data and so sees about 30% fewer text tokens. Vision therefore costs text little beyond the text data it displaces.

B.4 Held-out losses

We measure losses on two kinds of held-out data, both as per-token negative log-likelihood in nats. The held-out text and caption losses score unseen samples of the training distributions, and sections 4, 5.4 and F.3 use them. Out-of-distribution caption loss scores caption sets outside those distributions, and table 25 reports it.

In-distribution.

Held-out text loss is the per-token negative log-likelihood on held-out text from the training text corpus, weighted as in the training mixture. It is scored with the attention masking each model was trained with. Held-out caption loss is the per-token negative log-likelihood of the regenerated captions of MetaCLIP 1.2 images never used in training, so it samples the training caption distribution.

Out-of-distribution.

Out-of-distribution caption loss averages the caption loss of three sets of 5,000 images with equal weight: the COCO validation images with the first of their human reference captions (Lin et al., 2014), MetaCLIP 1.2 pairs with their original alt-text (Xu et al., 2024), and images from a licensed stock-photo collection. It is scored with the attention masking each model was trained with.

B.5 ImageNet linear probes

We use three linear probes on ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009). The downstream probe reads the multimodal model with all weights frozen. It mean-pools the backbone’s final normalized vision-token states and fits an ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularized linear classifier on 50 training images per class. A fixed 10% holdout selects the regularization strength from {10−4,10−3,10−2}\{10^{-4},10^{-3},10^{-2}\}, and the classifier is then refit on all 50,000 images. We report top-1 accuracy on the full validation split. The upstream probe (table 16) fits the same classifier to a frozen pretrained encoder before multimodal training. It mean-pools the encoder’s 256 final normalized patch tokens of a 224×224224\times 224 center crop; for WebSSL, it reads the exponential-moving-average teacher. The full-data probe applies the DINOv2 linear evaluation (Oquab et al., 2024) to the frozen pretrained encoder, training on the full ImageNet-1K training set. It gives the upstream accuracy in fig. 9 and section C.3.

D.3 Richer patch embeddings

The default encoder-free patch embedding is a single linear projection followed by RMSNorm and a learned gate (section A.1). We compare it with two richer patch embedding designs: a normalized two-layer projection inspired by Gemma 4 (Gemma Team, 2026), and a four-layer hierarchical MLP (Touvron et al., 2022) inspired by Inkling (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a). The lower part of table 21 describes each variant. The normalized two-layer projection changes patch size, resolution, position embeddings, and normalization together. It normalizes each patch with LayerNorm (Ba et al., 2016), projects it linearly, adds learned factorized 2D position embeddings, and then applies LayerNorm, a parameter-free RMSNorm, and a linear map into the backbone. The hierarchical MLP has four linear layers that fold neighboring pixels into channels in stages, with RMSNorm and GELU (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016) between them, a final RMSNorm, and no position embedding. In table 21, both richer variants read larger images in larger patches (768×768768\times 768 in 48×4848\times 48 patches and 640×640640\times 640 in 40×4040\times 40 patches, rather than 224×224224\times 224 in 14×1414\times 14 patches), so they produce the same 16×1616\times 16 grid of 256 vision tokens as the encoder. At 5.2×10215.2\times 10^{21} FLOPs, both narrow the gap to the encoder, and the hierarchical MLP matches it on Avg. VQA (table 21). The largest gain is on OCR and chart questions, where the default patch embedding trails the encoder most. Avg. Text is comparable across patch embeddings.

However, when training on 224×224224\times 224 images at 2.6×10212.6\times 10^{21} FLOPs, the two-layer projection gains 1.5 Avg. VQA over the default patch embedding whereas the hierarchical MLP loses 3.1, and both remain far behind the encoder (table 2). The hierarchical MLP helps only when it compresses a higher-resolution image into the same number of tokens. With 224×224224\times 224 instruction tuning, it matches the default patch embedding on 224×224224\times 224 images, while processing 640×640640\times 640 images into the same 256 tokens raises it to 38.8, mostly on OCR and chart questions (24.0 against 10.2). Raising only the instruction-tuning resolution to 448×448448\times 448 quadruples the tokens without compressing them, and the hierarchical MLP then gains 1.4 points, against 4.4 for the default patch embedding. The richer patch embeddings therefore help most with higher-resolution images.

D.4 Comparison with prior work

Prior work, Shukor et al. (2025), find that encoder-free models match or slightly outperform an encoder trained from scratch, whereas we find that the encoder leads (section 4). To investigate this discrepancy, we examine two choices in their setup that may work against the encoder, a reduced encoder learning rate and using the averaged validation loss. We also study a third difference, using alt-text captions rather than regenerated captions. First, we evaluate the runs of the scaling ladder (appendix G) on their averaged loss. We also retrain the ladder’s 0.6B and 1B backbones, sizes within the range of their study, with a reduced encoder learning rate, alt-text captions, or both (table 22). Every other setting matches the ladder’s runs, which serve as baselines.

Encoder learning rate.

Shukor et al. (2025) train their from-scratch encoder at a reduced learning rate, the best of the 0.1×0.1\times, 0.01×0.01\times, and 0.001×0.001\times multipliers they compare. We train the encoder at 0.01×0.01\times the backbone’s peak learning rate, and also at 0.1×0.1\times at 1B, with the projector at the full rate. Instruction tuning trains every encoder at its full rate. We find that lowering the rate shrinks the encoder’s lead (table 22), and most of the drop comes between the full rate and 0.1×0.1\times, whereas their sweep starts at 0.1×0.1\times and never trains the encoder at the full rate. At 0.01×0.01\times, the encoder is comparable to encoder-free on Avg. VQA at 1B and loses its caption-loss lead entirely at 0.6B.

Averaged validation loss.

Shukor et al. (2025) fit their scaling laws to validation loss averaged over interleaved, caption, and text data, with captions that are web alt-text. The text loss does not depend on the image, and in our ladder the interleaved loss barely differs between the encoder and encoder-free. Differences between vision components therefore have a weaker effect on the average, which makes it a noisier signal for comparing them. In our scaling ladder, the averaged loss barely separates the encoder from encoder-free, whereas held-out caption loss separates them clearly and tracks Avg. VQA (fig. 18). At 1.7B and 128 tokens per parameter, the two reach the same averaged loss while the encoder leads by 4.8 Avg. VQA points (fig. 15).

Alt-text captions.

We also train on the images’ original alt-text instead of the regenerated captions, for the encoder and encoder-free alike. This delays the encoder’s lead, as the two tie on alt-text caption loss up to 32 tokens per parameter. With both changes (a 0.01×0.01\times encoder learning rate and alt-text captions), encoder-free reaches a lower alt-text caption loss than the encoder at both sizes and every budget, by 0.04 to 0.07 nats, as Shukor et al. (2025) report. Overall, their finding may reflect an under-trained encoder or an averaged loss that can hide its benefit.

Appendix E In-fusion vision capacity

This section describes the in-fusion vision capacity variants of section 5, which add vision-only modules inside the backbone.

E.1 Implementation and sizing

In each augmented layer, in-fusion (FFN-only) adds a vision-only SwiGLU branch of width FF beside the shared FFN, reading the same normalized input. For backbone width DD and LaL_{a} augmented layers, it adds PFFN=La​(3​D​F+D)P_{\mathrm{FFN}}=L_{a}(3DF+D) parameters. In-fusion also adds zero-initialized vision-only query, key, value, and output projections with the shapes of the shared ones. For HQH_{Q} query heads, HK​VH_{KV} key–value heads, and head dimension dhd_{h}, they add PQKVO=2​La​D​dh​(HQ+HK​V)P_{\mathrm{QKVO}}=2L_{a}Dd_{h}(H_{Q}+H_{KV}) parameters. Attention runs once over the combined projections, so there is no second attention stream. Unless otherwise noted, every allocation augments the first eight layers (La=8L_{a}=8), and table 23 lists the resulting widths and parameter counts.

The depth ablation uses in-fusion (FFN-only) because its branch can be narrowed to fit the budget in any number of layers. Vision-only attention projections have the shapes of the shared ones, so in every layer they would take 0.35B of the 0.4B budget at 1.7B (28 layers) and 0.94B at 4B (36 layers), more than the whole budget.

E.2 Routing, depth, and attention-projection controls

In table 3, shared FFN widening grows the shared FFN of layers 1–8 from width 6,144 to 14,336. The FFN branches have width 8,192 when placed in eight layers and 2,304 when placed in all 28.

Routing at matched compute.

In-fusion (FFN-only) and the separate FFN branch differ only in which tokens use the branch. Because the all-token branch also runs on text tokens, it trains on fewer tokens at matched compute. Routing the branch to vision tokens leads on Avg. VQA at both budgets, while the all-token branch is slightly ahead on Avg. Text (table 24). At the longer budget, routing also raises downstream ImageNet probe accuracy from 61.2 to 66.0 (section B.5). With the same parameters, the separate FFN branch beats shared FFN widening on Avg. VQA (table 3).

Attention-projection controls.

In two 4B contrasts at matched training tokens, the vision-only attention projections improve visual understanding both on their own and alongside an FFN branch (table 25). The first adds only the attention projections of in-fusion to the encoder-free model, and the second compares in-fusion with a model that has only its FFN branch.

E.3 Comparison at longer training

At the longest training budget, 1.11T token-equivalents, in-fusion is comparable to the encoder on both Avg. Text and Avg. VQA at both model scales (table 26). In-fusion (FFN-only) is comparable to the encoder at 1.7B and slightly behind it on Avg. VQA at 4B, where it also trails in-fusion at every budget (fig. 5).

E.4 Where vision tokens are processed

To see where each design processes vision tokens, we probe the 1.7B models at the longest training budget (fig. 16), adapting the probes of Chen et al. (2026). For each backbone block, we measure how much the vision tokens change as one minus the cosine similarity between their hidden state before and after the block, and how much attention caption tokens place on them. In both in-fusion models, vision tokens change mostly in the blocks with vision-only modules and little after them. The encoder-free model keeps changing them through its early and middle shared blocks. The encoder’s tokens enter the backbone already processed, so they change mostly in the first few blocks. After the in-fusion blocks, caption tokens attend to vision tokens more than in the encoder and encoder-free models. The same pattern holds at a fifth of the training budget. These probes suggest that in-fusion capacity performs vision-specific processing in its own early blocks and passes stable vision tokens to the shared backbone, whereas an encoder-free model builds them up across its shared layers.

Appendix G Scaling ladder

Section 5.4 tests whether the comparisons of sections 4 and 5 hold as the backbone grows, using a ladder of backbone sizes. This section gives the ladder’s setup, the scaling laws fitted to it, and how well the laws predict runs they were not fitted on.

Setup.

The ladder trains the encoder-free, encoder, and in-fusion recipes under the protocol of section 2 on backbones from 0.6B to 6.4B parameters. The backbones follow the architecture of the 1.7B backbone, with query heads of dimension 128 spanning the hidden size, half as many key–value heads, and a feed-forward width three times the hidden size. The vision module grows with the backbone (table 28). The encoder keeps the proportions of the 1.7B pairing: half the backbone’s hidden size dd, one layer fewer than the backbone, an MLP four times its own width, and round​(0.75​d/128)\mathrm{round}(0.75\,d/128) attention heads of dimension 128. Its parameter count therefore stays at a nearly fixed ratio to the backbone’s non-embedding parameters. The in-fusion modules occupy the first round​(8​L/28)\mathrm{round}(8L/28) of the backbone’s LL layers, 29% of the depth, as at 1.7B. Their widths are set so that they match the encoder’s parameter count.

All recipes at a backbone size share one peak learning rate and one batch size (table 28). The peak learning rate is 3×10−4​1.72×109/Ntot3\times 10^{-4}\sqrt{1.72\times 10^{9}/N_{\mathrm{tot}}}, rounded, where NtotN_{\mathrm{tot}} is the total backbone parameter count. The batch size grows by about 1.5 times per backbone size. Warmup lasts 2 tokens per non-embedding backbone parameter (2 TPP), e.g., 2.8B tokens for the 1.7B backbone, which has 1.4B non-embedding parameters. The other settings follow table 8. The 1.7B and 4B runs of sections 3, 4 and 5 instead keep a batch of 1,024 sequences and 4,000 warmup updates at both sizes. At 1.7B, where the ladder’s batch is also 1,024, each ladder recipe is within two Avg. VQA points of those runs when interpolated to their budgets (sections 4 and 5).

Each recipe and size has one constant-learning-rate run, decayed over the final 10% of training at several budgets (table 29). Each point in figs. 7 and 19 is one decayed endpoint. At 1.7B, the ladder’s encoder is the 0.4B encoder of section 2. At 6.4B, we also train the encoder recipe with the 0.4B encoder of the main runs, to check that this smaller encoder does not limit larger backbones (section A.2). Table 29 lists the downstream scores of every run the laws are fitted on.

Scaling laws.

For Avg. VQA, caption loss, and text loss, we fit a separate law for each recipe. For the losses it takes the form L​(N,D)=E+A​N−α+B​D−βL(N,D)=E+A\,N^{-\alpha}+B\,D^{-\beta} (Hoffmann et al., 2022), with NN the non-embedding backbone parameters and DD the token-equivalents (section 2.3), fitted by minimizing a Huber loss on log loss. For Avg. VQA, it is linear in ln⁡N\ln N and ln⁡D\ln D, fitted by least squares. Each is fitted on the recipe’s 17 ladder runs (table 30). From 1.7B to 6.4B, encoder-free needs 2.6 to 3.1 times the encoder’s compute on Avg. VQA, 2.4 to 3.8 times on caption loss, and about the same on text loss. In-fusion needs about the same compute as the encoder on Avg. VQA and text loss, and slightly less on caption loss. Table 31 gives the scaling laws’ errors on every run and on each left-out backbone size. Fitted on the ladder alone, the caption-loss laws also predict the separately trained 1.7B and 4B runs of sections 3, 4 and 5 with an average absolute error of 1.6% (table 32). Their warmup differs from the ladder’s, and at 4B, so do the batch size and the size of the vision module. Vision learning rate.

Table 33 uses the same peak learning rate for every parameter. Table 34 instead adjusts the learning rate of the vision path alone, while every other parameter keeps the shared rate. A higher vision learning rate brings the from-scratch encoder to within a point of in-fusion and partially closes MetaCLIP’s gap to the from-scratch encoder, but the from-scratch encoder and in-fusion still lead.

H.2 Training time

Here, we compare the training time of the encoder recipe with encoder-free, in-fusion (FFN-only), and in-fusion. Training time can be compared in two ways: per-step comparisons fix the number of optimizer updates, whereas equal-FLOP comparisons fix total modeled training compute. Because encoder computation counts toward that budget, the encoder recipe completes fewer updates at equal FLOPs, so its equal-FLOP time premium is smaller than its per-step premium.

We measure training time with complete optimizer updates on H200 GPUs with fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) (Zhao et al., 2023). The matched 4B comparison in table 35 runs the four recipes on 32 GPUs with a global batch of 1,024 sequences. Each row projects training time from measured steady-state update times to the same modeled lifetime compute, 1.04×10221.04\times 10^{22} FLOPs (400B token-equivalents at 4B; section A.5).

Table 35 times the encoder and the in-fusion configurations of table 23, which match the encoder’s 0.4B vision-only parameters, under the 4B training setup above. At equal lifetime compute, neither in-fusion variant measurably changes training time relative to encoder-free. The encoder takes 2.9% longer than encoder-free and 2.6% longer than in-fusion at equal FLOPs. Per step, the encoder takes 5.3% longer than encoder-free. Note that the encoder used here is an unoptimized reference implementation, and encoder-specific optimization can narrow its gap. For instance, a compiled (Ansel et al., 2024) version of the Base encoder in table 5 trains within 0.2% of an in-fusion (FFN-only) model with the same vision-only parameters at 4B.

Encoder pipelining.

Overlapping or pipelining (Huang et al., 2019) the encoder recovers little of its cost. At 4B, running the next microbatch’s encoder forward pass alongside the backbone hides 20–36% of the encoder’s per-step cost. Only the forward pass overlaps, because the encoder’s backward pass waits for the backbone’s gradients. With or without an encoder, a four-stage pipeline has about half the throughput of the encoder recipe under FSDP on the same 32 GPUs. FSDP optimizations applied to the encoder alone, such as prefetching parameters or skipping gradient synchronization between accumulation steps, change step time by less than 0.7%.

Visual workload.

Per step, encoder-free and in-fusion (FFN-only) both train faster than the encoder recipe. Encoder-free saves more because the vision-only FFNs of in-fusion (FFN-only) cost about 95% of the encoder’s FLOPs. In an 8-GPU setup at 1.7B, raising the proportion of image–text data from 10% to 50% widens encoder-free’s saving from 10.0% to 13.2%, while in-fusion (FFN-only) saves 6–7% throughout (fig. 20).

H.3 Inference latency

Section 6.3 compares how fast each recipe serves image requests. We run every design in our own implementation on one H200, so all designs share the same inference code. Each request has one image and 256 text tokens and generates 120 tokens. Largely following the inference benchmark setup of Mono-InternVL (Luo et al., 2025b), we report time to first token (TTFT) and output throughput with 16 concurrent requests and 448-pixel images (1,024 vision tokens) unless noted. Each configuration is measured in four runs, and we report medians with full ranges.

Without a separate encoder, the backbone no longer waits for each image to be encoded, so TTFT falls (fig. 21). In-fusion (FFN-only) still processes every vision token with its vision-only FFNs, and at matched vision-only parameters, it performs approximately the same computation per image as the encoder. Its advantage comes from running in eight wide layers instead of the encoder’s deeper stack of narrower layers (27 at the 0.4B budget), in our eager-mode implementation. The inference time saving grows with resolution, because more vision tokens make the encoder a larger share of the time to first token.

Varying the vision budget.

We also try varying the vision-only parameters across the encoder sizes of section A.2, with both in-fusion variants sized to match each encoder (table 36). In-fusion is faster than the encoder at every budget. The time that vision adds over encoder-free is set by the vision budget rather than the backbone, so in-fusion (FFN-only) saves as much time at 4B as at 1.7B. Its relative inference time saving is smaller at 4B only because the backbone’s own prefill time is longer.
